definitions.plain: The luck of finding one good thing while looking for another.
definitions.poetic: The wrong turning that pays better than the road that was planned.
definitions.riddle: Hunt one treasure and I slip a better one into your pocket, unasked.

etymology: Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754, out of a Persian fairy tale, for a talent he thought English had no name for.
usage: By pure ___, the missing letter turned up inside a borrowed book.

definitions.plain: A strong longing to travel and see far places.
definitions.poetic: The itch that packs a bag before the mind has agreed to go.
definitions.riddle: No kitchen can feed me; only a horizon quiets me, and never for long.

etymology: Borrowed whole from German in the first years of the twentieth century, at the height of a fashion for walking tours.
usage: Her ___ flared with every train whistle that crossed the valley.

definitions.plain: A bittersweet longing for times gone by.
definitions.poetic: The past, seen through the one window that opens only from this side.
definitions.riddle: The farther you sail from a shore, the sweeter I make it look.

etymology: Coined in 1688 as a medical diagnosis — Swiss soldiers pining in foreign camps, said to be curable only by going home.
usage: The smell of woodsmoke filled him with ___ for his grandfather’s cabin.

definitions.plain: A sudden moment of understanding that changes everything.
definitions.poetic: Lightning indoors: one flash, and the whole room of the mind is lit.
definitions.riddle: I arrive uninvited in bathtubs and on staircases, and after me nothing looks the same.

etymology: From the Greek for ‘a showing forth’, once reserved for divine appearances and a feast on the sixth of January.
usage: Halfway through washing the dishes she had an ___ about the unfinished poem.

definitions.plain: A gentle, lingering sadness with no single cause.
definitions.poetic: Rain that falls inside a person while the sky stays dry.
definitions.riddle: Too soft to be grief, too heavy to be rest — I am the blue hour of the heart.

etymology: From the Greek for black bile, one of the four humours once thought to govern the temper.
usage: A pleasant ___ settled on the porch as the last light left the garden.

definitions.plain: The state of being alone, especially by choice and at peace.
definitions.poetic: Aloneness worn as a warm coat rather than a wound.
definitions.riddle: Crowds destroy me, and yet I am no enemy of the ones you love.

etymology: From the Latin for alone — a monastic word for centuries before it became a comfortable one.
usage: He kept Sunday mornings for ___, tea, and the slow crossword.

definitions.plain: Playful, fanciful humour; a taste for odd and charming notions.
definitions.poetic: The soap-bubble logic by which a teapot might well be a house for wrens.
definitions.riddle: I turn umbrellas into rowboats and errands into expeditions, and I weigh nothing at all.

etymology: A softened form of a seventeenth-century nonsense word for a fanciful trifle, cousin to ‘flim-flam’.
usage: The garden gnomes wearing tiny scarves were pure ___ on her part.

definitions.plain: A pleasant daydream; the state of being lost in dreamy thought.
definitions.poetic: The little rowboat the mind takes out when nobody is asking it to steer.
definitions.riddle: Your eyes stay open while I carry you elsewhere; a dropped teacup calls you back.

etymology: From an old French word for wild rejoicing and rambling talk; crossing the Channel, it grew quiet and dreamy.
usage: The lecture dissolved into a ___ about lighthouses and summer storms.

definitions.plain: A treasured object handed down through a family for generations.
definitions.poetic: A thing that outlives its owners and keeps the fingerprints of hands now gone.
definitions.riddle: At auction I fetch almost nothing; on a mantelpiece I am the whole family.

etymology: Middle English joined an inherited estate to an old word for a tool — the family implement that passed on with the land.
usage: The clock in the hall was the only ___ that survived the move.

definitions.plain: A gentle song sung to send a child to sleep.
definitions.poetic: A small tune with a door in it, opening onto sleep.
definitions.riddle: Sing me badly and I work just as well; my audience is already half gone.

etymology: In English since the sixteenth century, and imitative at both ends: the sound came first and the spelling was fitted to it.
usage: She hummed the same ___ her grandmother had hummed to her.

definitions.plain: To speak very softly, using breath instead of voice.
definitions.poetic: Words with their shoes off, crossing a quiet room.
definitions.riddle: Raise me and I stop being myself.

etymology: Old English, imitative — the word sounds like the thing it names, as its cousins in Dutch and German also do.
usage: A ___ went round the reading room, and then the hush came back.

definitions.plain: The strip of floor beneath a doorway; the point where something begins.
definitions.poetic: The line a house draws between itself and the weather.
definitions.riddle: Cross me and you have arrived, though you have not yet gone anywhere.

etymology: Old English for the sill of a door; the second half of the word is a puzzle even to scholars.
usage: He paused on the ___ with the letter still unopened.

definitions.plain: A case of glass and metal that carries a flame safely from place to place.
definitions.poetic: A small tame piece of the sun, given a handle.
definitions.riddle: Carry me and the dark steps back exactly as far as I say, and not one pace further.

etymology: From an old Greek word for a torch, arriving by way of Latin and French; for centuries English misspelled it after the thin horn panes that glazed it.
usage: She hung the ___ on the gate so the late walker would find the path.

definitions.plain: Small dry sticks and shavings used to start a fire.
definitions.poetic: The little sacrifice a fire requires before it will agree to be a fire.
definitions.riddle: I am the smallest thing in the woodshed, and nothing there burns without me.

etymology: From an Old Norse verb for setting alight — the same root the language uses when a feeling catches rather than a log.
usage: He split the ___ finer than it needed, because the doing of it was restful.

definitions.plain: A small piece of coal or wood still glowing after the flame has gone out.
definitions.poetic: The last red eye of a fire, watching the room until morning.
definitions.riddle: The poker hunts for me at midnight; the bellows can still talk me into a flame.

etymology: Old English for a smouldering cinder, with cousins in Old Norse and German — one of the oldest fire-words the language still uses.
usage: She banked the ___ under ash so the morning would have somewhere to begin.

definitions.plain: The floor of a fireplace, and by extension the fireside as the centre of a home.
definitions.poetic: The one stone in a house that has been warm every winter since the house was built.
definitions.riddle: Build a house around me and it becomes a home; leave me cold and it is only shelter.

etymology: Old English, and the same word in German; the family name for the fireplace floor is older than the chimney that now stands over it.
usage: Every chair in the room had been turned to face the ___.

definitions.plain: Timber that the sea has carried, worn smooth, and left along the tideline.
definitions.poetic: A branch that went to sea a tree and came back a sculpture.
definitions.riddle: The tide hands me over and takes me back for years before I am dry enough to burn.

etymology: Recorded in English since the seventeenth century, though the beachcombers who lived off it never needed the word written down.
usage: He fed the fire with ___ and the flames burned a strange salt green.

definitions.plain: A small object held on to only because of the person or place it recalls.
definitions.poetic: A pebble, a ticket stub, a button: none of them beautiful, all of them evidence.
definitions.riddle: Usually ugly, always small — and I am the first thing carried out of a burning house.

etymology: First written in the 1790s, when English was fond of compounds that name a thing by the errand it runs.
usage: She carried the button as a ___, though she never said whose coat it came from.

definitions.plain: A plot of ground planted with fruit trees and kept for their crop.
definitions.poetic: A wood set out in rows by someone who did not expect to eat from it.
definitions.riddle: Every autumn I pay my rent in apples, and I am the only forest that was ever arranged.

etymology: Old English joined a word for a garden herb to the enclosure it grew in; the trees arrived later and kept the name.
usage: The old ___ still sets fruit, though nobody has pruned it since the war.

definitions.plain: An instrument with a magnetised needle that shows which way is north.
definitions.poetic: One nervous sliver of iron in a dish of glass, insisting on the north.
definitions.riddle: Spin me, shake me, take me down a mine: I will still point at the same cold country.

etymology: From an old verb for stepping round a circle — the jointed legs that draw one share the name, and sailors borrowed it from geometry.
usage: The ___ in the hall case points a little east of north, and always has.

definitions.plain: The blank border of a page, outside the written or printed text.
definitions.poetic: The white field around the words, where a reader is allowed to argue.
definitions.riddle: Printers give me away for nothing, and every good reader fills me with a second book.

etymology: From the Latin for an edge, the same root behind the word for a frontier province — a border in both senses.
usage: Every book he lent came back with the ___ full of his pencilled quarrels.

definitions.plain: A small pot set into a desk to hold what a pen is dipped in.
definitions.poetic: A black pool let into oak, from which whole libraries were drawn up a drop at a time.
definitions.riddle: Dip and dip again: I hold about two hundred words, and then I want filling.

etymology: A nineteenth-century desk word; before it, the pot stood loose on the table, or hung from the belt as a horn.
usage: The ___ in the study desk still has a crust of black at the bottom.

definitions.plain: A yearly book of calendars, tides, moon phases, and weather predictions.
definitions.poetic: A whole year bound in advance, with the moon’s appointments already kept.
definitions.riddle: I tell a farmer when to sow and a sailor when the water will be high, and by January I am waste paper.

etymology: Reached English through medieval Latin from Arabic; the Arabic word itself is disputed, which pleases lexicographers more than it should.
usage: The ___ hanging by the door had every frost of the last decade underlined.

definitions.plain: A hinged leather bag with a nozzle, worked by hand to blow air on a fire.
definitions.poetic: A pair of leather lungs kept on a hook beside the grate.
definitions.riddle: Squeeze me and the coals go from grey to gold; I breathe only while somebody else does the work.

etymology: The plural of an old word for a leather bag; the singular went out of use and the pair kept working.
usage: Two puffs of the ___ and the kitchen fire took hold.

definitions.plain: The dusty tangle a spider leaves behind in a corner nobody sweeps.
definitions.poetic: Lace that no one ordered, hung in the one corner the broom forgives.
definitions.riddle: Dust makes me visible and the maid makes me temporary; my builder moved out months ago.

etymology: The spider’s older English name survives nowhere else in the language: it hides in this one compound, and nobody notices.
usage: A ___ across the door meant nobody had come this way since spring.

definitions.plain: The handrail of a staircase, and the row of uprights that holds it up.
definitions.poetic: The part of a staircase that was built to be touched.
definitions.riddle: Children ride me down; the old are grateful for me going up. What am I?

etymology: A slurred form of the word for a pomegranate flower — the little swelling posts were carved in that shape, and the name slid down the stair.
usage: She took the stairs two at a time with one hand on the ___.

definitions.plain: A figure of straw and old clothes set in a field to frighten birds.
definitions.poetic: Two poles, one shirt, and just enough suggestion of a man to keep a field honest.
definitions.riddle: Hired for my outline alone, and by August the rooks have worked me out.

etymology: In English since the 1550s, when it also meant a thin and ragged person — an insult before it was a fixture of the fields.
usage: The ___ gave up its hat in the March gales and never got another.

definitions.plain: An outline portrait filled in solid black; any shape seen against the light.
definitions.poetic: A person reduced to their edge, and still recognisable, which is the unsettling part.
definitions.riddle: Cut me from black paper in four minutes for a shilling: I was the photograph before there were photographs.

etymology: Named in mockery for a French finance minister whose economies were thought as cheap and as thin as the paper cuttings.
usage: Her ___ was cut at a fair in 1911 and has hung in the hall ever since.

definitions.plain: A sound thrown back from a surface and heard again a moment later.
definitions.poetic: The hill’s habit of repeating a shout with all the courage taken out of it.
definitions.riddle: Call at a cliff and I answer in your own voice, a little later and a little less. What am I?

etymology: From the Greek word for a sound, carried into Latin and French and arriving unchanged — a word that behaved like the thing it names.
usage: The ___ in the empty ballroom answered every footstep twice.

definitions.plain: To follow a winding course, as a river does across a flat valley.
definitions.poetic: The river’s refusal to be a line, written in loops across a hundred fields.
definitions.riddle: The water prefers me: I am the longest distance between two points.

etymology: From the Greek name of a river in Asia Minor so famously crooked that geographers still borrow its name for every bend they map.
usage: Let the lane ___ if it likes; there is no hurry before supper.

definitions.plain: The space under a roof, used for storage and reached by a ladder.
definitions.poetic: Bars of dust-lit air under the rafters, and a smell of paper kept warm for fifty summers.
definitions.riddle: Every family sends somebody up into me at Christmas, and nobody stays longer than the errand.

etymology: Named for a style of Greek architecture — a low decorative storey above the cornice, which builders promptly filled with boxes.
usage: The ___ ladder came down with a groan and a fall of forty years of dust.

definitions.plain: The gathering in of a ripe crop, and the season in which it is gathered.
definitions.poetic: The one fortnight of the year when a whole village goes to bed aching and pleased.
definitions.riddle: The moon in September was given a name of its own on my account.

etymology: Old English for autumn itself; the season handed its word over to the work, and borrowed a French one for the leaves.
usage: The ___ was in by the ninth, and the whole valley slept.

definitions.plain: A small beetle whose body makes a cold greenish light on summer nights.
definitions.poetic: A spark that can be caught in two hands without harm, and goes out when the jar is shut.
definitions.riddle: I am a beetle pretending to be a lantern, and I do it in order to be married.

etymology: An English compound of the 1650s, wrong twice over: the insect is neither what the first half of its name claims nor what the second half does.
usage: One ___ came in at the window and the whole room went quiet to watch it.

definitions.plain: Fruit brought down by the weather; by extension, any gain that arrives unearned.
definitions.poetic: The apples the storm has decided are nobody’s, lying bruised and free in the wet grass.
definitions.riddle: I arrive by weather and never by work, and nobody has ever refused me.

etymology: From English forest law: what the weather delivered could be taken away, while everything still standing belonged to the lord.
usage: The legacy was a ___, and she spent every penny of it on the roof.

definitions.plain: The earthy smell of rain falling on dry ground.
definitions.poetic: Dust’s one answer to rain, and it arrives before the thunder does.
definitions.riddle: Thirsty stone drinks, and I am born of it; you smell me before you hear the storm.

etymology: Coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists, who traced the smell to an oil that plants shed into dry clay and rock.
usage: After the drought broke, the whole street smelled of ___.

definitions.plain: Twilight; the fading light just after sunset.
definitions.poetic: The blue seam where day is stitched quietly into night.
definitions.riddle: Neither lamp nor dark, I am the hour when bats and porch lights wake together.

etymology: Old English by way of Scots, and kept alive mainly by northern songs long after the rest of England settled on ‘twilight’.
usage: Children were called in from the ___ one by one.

definitions.plain: Calm, peaceful, and golden — used of remembered happy times.
definitions.poetic: Weather borrowed from a kinder year, kept pressed between the mind’s pages.
definitions.riddle: I nest on a flat sea in midwinter and make the storms wait their turn.

etymology: The Greeks held that a certain sea-bird nested on the winter water, and that the gods flattened the waves for a fortnight while it did.
usage: They spoke of the ___ summers before the mill closed.

definitions.plain: Sweet and smooth to hear, like a flowing voice or melody.
definitions.poetic: Speech that pours slow and amber, coating the ear like warm honey.
definitions.riddle: I describe the voice you would follow into a third hour of the story.

etymology: From the Latin for honey and for flowing — a compliment first paid to the sermons of saints.
usage: The announcer’s ___ baritone made even the shipping news soothing.

definitions.plain: The soft partial shadow around the edge of a full shadow.
definitions.poetic: The grey hem where shadow frays into light, and neither side will own the border.
definitions.riddle: In an eclipse I am the almost: not the bite of darkness, only its breath.

etymology: Coined by the astronomer Kepler from the Latin for ‘almost’ and ‘shadow’.
usage: The cat slept at the edge of the lamplight, half gold, half grey, in the ___.

definitions.plain: Nobly impractical; chasing ideals without regard for reality.
definitions.poetic: Armoured in daydreams, riding out to rescue what never asked for saving.
definitions.riddle: I tilt at windmills and call them giants; sensible people sigh at me, and secretly cheer.

etymology: The novel is 1605; the adjective is 1791 — it took the language two centuries to admit that it needed the word.
usage: Restoring the ruined lighthouse by hand was a ___ project, and he began anyway.

definitions.plain: A soft whispering or rustling sound.
definitions.poetic: The hush the poplars pass along, leaf to leaf, like a secret.
definitions.riddle: The wind lowers its voice to a library hush, and the sound it makes then is me.

etymology: Latin, an imitative word — say it slowly and you hear the sound it names.
usage: A ___ of turning pages filled the reading room.

definitions.plain: Lasting for a day or an afternoon; gone almost as soon as it is noticed.
definitions.poetic: Beautiful the way frost-flowers are beautiful: gone by the time the kettle sings.
definitions.riddle: Mayflies, rainbows, and perfect snowballs all swear allegiance to me.

etymology: From the Greek for ‘lasting a day’, said first of fevers, then of mayflies, then of everything dear.
usage: Chalk art is ___ by nature; the afternoon rain took the whole mural.

definitions.plain: A manuscript page reused after the earlier writing was scraped away, with traces left.
definitions.poetic: A page that keeps its ghosts: old ink dreaming under the new.
definitions.riddle: Scrape me and rewrite me — still the first story rises through the second like a watermark.

etymology: From the Greek for ‘scraped again’: parchment was dear, so monks rubbed the old letters away and wrote atop the shadow.
usage: The city is a ___, Roman stones showing through the medieval walls.

definitions.plain: A long, pointless, complicated procedure or ramble of talk.
definitions.poetic: A corridor of little doors between a person and the one simple thing they came for.
definitions.riddle: Fill in form nine to request form twelve: I am the dance, never the destination.

etymology: From a medieval parchment of names and seals so long that its title came to mean any tedious catalogue.
usage: Renewing the permit was a two-hour ___ of stamps and queues.

definitions.plain: A recessed seat beside a hearth, set inside the chimney’s own corner.
definitions.poetic: The warmest square yard in an English house, and the hardest to leave.
definitions.riddle: Sit in me and the fire is no longer across the room. The fire is family.

etymology: Two old northern words that have only been one word for three centuries; both halves are still alive on their own in Scotland.
usage: They took their tea in the ___ and let the weather do as it liked.

definitions.plain: A spell of listlessness; a stretch of time in which nothing moves.
definitions.poetic: A becalmed week with the sails up and no wind willing to bother.
definitions.riddle: Sailors named me for a windless sea. You meet me on a Tuesday afternoon.

etymology: From an old word for a dullard, pluralised by sailors into a belt of the Atlantic where the trade winds simply give up.
usage: February found the whole house in the ___, cat included.

definitions.plain: Notes, arguments, and drawings written by readers in the borders of a book.
definitions.poetic: The conversation a book has with everyone who has held it, conducted in pencil.
definitions.riddle: Libraries fine you for me; scholars have spent whole careers reading nothing else.

etymology: Latin in dress but modern in use — a nineteenth-century name for a habit as old as parchment, and Coleridge’s best work is filed under it.
usage: The second-hand copy came with a stranger’s ___ arguing at every chapter.

definitions.plain: Fine floating cobweb seen in autumn air; anything as light and thin as that.
definitions.poetic: Whole fields of spider silk let go at once, drifting like the ghost of a fleece.
definitions.riddle: Look along the stubble on a bright November morning: the entire field is strung with me.

etymology: Recorded from the fourteenth century for the threads of a mild autumn; the compound behind it has been argued over ever since.
usage: The hedge was hung with ___ and every strand held its own drop of mist.

definitions.plain: Delicate ornamental work made of fine twisted gold or silver wire.
definitions.poetic: Metal persuaded to behave like lace by a jeweller with small pliers and no hurry.
definitions.riddle: Look at me through a lens or do not look at me at all: my whole argument is made at one millimetre.

etymology: From the Latin words for thread and for grain — the two things the jeweller’s wire is drawn out and beaded into.
usage: The locket’s ___ had blackened, and no cloth would reach into it.

definitions.plain: The green crust that forms on copper and bronze left out in the weather.
definitions.poetic: The colour a roof turns when it stops being metal and starts being landscape.
definitions.riddle: Every cathedral dome comes to me in the end; I am what rust would be if it had taste.

etymology: Old French named the colour after the country supposed to produce it; the phrase collapsed into a single word by the fourteenth century.
usage: The ___ on the weathervane had spread until the arrow was as green as the copper beech.

definitions.plain: A warm brown pigment, and the brown tone of early photographs.
definitions.poetic: The colour every old photograph agrees to become, whatever it was on the day.
definitions.riddle: I began in the ink sac of a cuttlefish and ended up meaning ‘the past’.

etymology: Greek for the cuttlefish itself; artists ground its ink for centuries before photographers borrowed both the colour and the name.
usage: In the hall portrait, ___ has softened everyone into the same brown family.

definitions.plain: A flock of starlings in flight, moving as one shape over a winter roost.
definitions.poetic: Ten thousand birds behaving like a single animal, and not one bird in charge of it.
definitions.riddle: Sunset over a pier in November, and the sky pours itself from shape to shape: what has the sky become?

etymology: One of the fifteenth-century company-nouns collected for gentlemen’s sport — the same list that gave us the exaltation of larks.
usage: The whole village came down to the pier at dusk to watch the ___.

definitions.plain: A soft warm breeze, especially one out of the west.
definitions.poetic: Wind at its gentlest: enough to move a curtain, not enough to turn a page.
definitions.riddle: Sailors curse me for arriving instead of a real wind; a hammock in August is all I am good for.

etymology: The Greeks made the west wind a god and the Romans kept him on the payroll; the god has gone and the breeze still has his name.
usage: A ___ came off the water and lifted the corner of the tablecloth.

definitions.plain: The white feathery ice that grows on grass and railings on a still, cold night.
definitions.poetic: A night’s worth of ice grown in fern shapes on every blade and wire in the field.
definitions.riddle: Not snow, and I never fell: I grew where I stand, out of the air, between midnight and six.

etymology: In English since the fourteenth century, and known to most readers through the translators of Exodus, who needed a name for what lay on the desert ground at dawn.
usage: The lawn was stiff with ___ and every footprint stayed until noon.

definitions.plain: Either of the two days in the year when the sun reaches its farthest point from the equator.
definitions.poetic: The day the sun climbs no higher and hangs there, apparently thinking it over.
definitions.riddle: Twice a year I stop the sun in its tracks for three mornings together. What day am I?

etymology: Latin, borrowed by astronomers in the thirteenth century; before them, farmers simply called the days by their feasts.
usage: The stones line up on the ___, and half the county comes to stand in the mud and see it.

definitions.plain: Using very few words; terse to the point of bluntness.
definitions.poetic: A reply short enough to fit on a coin and sharp enough to end the argument.
definitions.riddle: A king threatened a city: ‘If I enter, I will level it.’ The city sent back one word — ‘If.’ What kind of answer is that?

etymology: From the Greek name of the region whose soldiers were famous for answering at the shortest available length.
usage: His ___ note said only: ‘Roof mended. Cat unimpressed.’

definitions.plain: A heap of stones piled up as a landmark, a boundary, or a memorial.
definitions.poetic: The only monument a walker can build in ten minutes, out of whatever is lying about.
definitions.riddle: Add a stone to me as you pass and I will still be pointing the way in a hundred years.

etymology: From Gaelic — one of the few words the hills gave to English, rather than the other way about.
usage: They built a ___ at the col, where the path stops being obvious.

definitions.plain: Sea spray torn from the tops of waves and blown along the surface by a gale.
definitions.poetic: The sea’s own smoke, streaming off the crests in long white ropes.
definitions.riddle: In a full gale I make the difference between a grey sea and a white one, and I never quite come down.

etymology: A Scots sea-word that reached English through nineteenth-century poets, who liked the sound of it rather more than the sailors did.
usage: The ferry crossed in a smother of ___ and everybody stayed below.

definitions.plain: Wreckage or cargo found floating after a ship has gone down.
definitions.poetic: What the sea gives back of a ship, in no order, over several weeks.
definitions.riddle: The lawyers keep me apart from my brother: he was thrown overboard on purpose, and I was not.

etymology: A term of Old French sea-law, in English by the sixteenth century; the distinction it draws decided who owned a wreck.
usage: The tideline was a museum of ___: crate boards, one shoe, a doll’s arm.

definitions.plain: A poem or song for the dawn, especially one for lovers parting at daybreak.
definitions.poetic: The song sung under a window at first light, with the singer already late for the road.
definitions.riddle: Sing my opposite at a cradle and my own kind at a window: the difference between us is only the hour.

etymology: From an Old French word for daybreak; the Provençal poets were writing the form for a century before anyone gave it a name.
usage: He wrote her an ___ that mentioned the milk cart twice.

definitions.plain: A travelling case that opens into two equal halves; also a word made by fusing two.
definitions.poetic: Two words folded into one suitcase, with the hinges still showing if the light is right.
definitions.riddle: Buckle two meanings into one trunk and the strap still shows. What is such a word called?

etymology: The bag came from French in the sixteenth century; the second sense was invented in 1871 by a mathematician writing about a looking-glass.
usage: ‘Smog’ is a ___, and so is the name the twins finally agreed on for the pony.

definitions.plain: Belonging to a threshold; occupying the space between one state and the next.
definitions.poetic: The corridor between two rooms, the hour between two days, the year between two names.
definitions.riddle: The waiting room, the ferry, the last hour before a wedding: all of them are mine.

etymology: From the Latin for a doorway’s sill, taken up a century ago by anthropologists for the middle stage of any rite.
usage: The hall at dusk felt ___ — no longer day, and not yet lamps.

definitions.plain: An order requiring people to be indoors by a stated hour of the night.
definitions.poetic: A bell rung at eight that turns a whole town into a set of lit windows.
definitions.riddle: I began as an order about banking the coals and ended as an order about being home.

etymology: Norman French, an instruction shouted at nightfall about the household fire; the bell that carried it outlived the rule by six centuries.
usage: The old ___ bell still rings at eight, and nobody now goes in when it does.

definitions.plain: A glass building on a great house, built to winter tender fruit trees under cover.
definitions.poetic: A greenhouse with pretensions: sash windows, a stove, and a hundred trees in tubs.
definitions.riddle: Wheel the citrus into me in October and out again in May; I was a rich man’s way of owning a warmer country.

etymology: A seventeenth-century fashion imported from France and Holland, when a heated glass house was the most expensive way to show off in Europe.
usage: The ___ has lost four panes and gained a fig tree that nobody planted.

definitions.plain: The treatment of light and shade in a picture, especially in strong contrast.
definitions.poetic: One candle, one face, and a great deal of confident darkness doing the rest.
definitions.riddle: Rembrandt lit a single cheek and left the whole canvas to me; I am mostly shadow and all of the drama.

etymology: Italian, and a studio word long before it was a critical one — painters used it for a workshop technique two centuries before historians made it a virtue.
usage: The portrait is nearly all ___: a hand, half a collar, and one very tired eye.

definitions.plain: A fine writing surface made from calfskin, smoother and paler than parchment.
definitions.poetic: A page that was once an animal, scraped and stretched until it could hold a thousand years of ink.
definitions.riddle: Acts of Parliament were still printed on me long after paper was cheap, because paper is not trusted to last.

etymology: From an Old French word for a calf; the trade name outlived the trade, and printers still use it for their best paper.
usage: The charter is on ___, and its ink is blacker than anything the last century managed.

definitions.plain: A navigator’s instrument that measures the angle between a star and the horizon.
definitions.poetic: A brass wedge of a thing that turns one careful glance at the sun into a place on the ocean.
definitions.riddle: Give me the noon sun and a good clock and I will tell you where in the world you are standing.

etymology: An eighteenth-century improvement on older sea-instruments; its arc, its mirrors and its shade glasses are unchanged in the ones carried today.
usage: He kept the ___ in its mahogany box and took it out twice a year to be admired.

definitions.plain: The illustration facing the title page at the beginning of a book.
definitions.poetic: The one picture a book puts on before it will say its own name.
definitions.riddle: Open the cover, turn a single leaf, and I am looking at the title from across the gutter.

etymology: An architect’s word for the face of a building, taken over by printers in the seventeenth century and never given back.
usage: The ___ shows the author at forty, looking as though he suspects the reader.

definitions.plain: To gather what the harvesters left in a field; to pick up scattered facts.
definitions.poetic: The right, once written into custom, to walk a cut field and take whatever the rake missed.
definitions.riddle: Ruth did it in a barley field; a scholar does it in footnotes. What is the verb?

etymology: Old French, and probably Celtic before that; the practice was defended by custom for centuries and finally ruled against in an English court in 1788.
usage: She would ___ the last of the barley rows while the light held.

definitions.plain: Happening every day; ordinary to the point of going unnoticed.
definitions.poetic: The kettle, the post, the same three stairs that always creak: a life’s true furniture.
definitions.riddle: Doctors once used me of a fever that returned at the same hour daily; now I mean only Tuesday.

etymology: Latin, and a physician’s word first — fevers were sorted by how often they came back, and this was the one that always did.
usage: The ___ business of the house — coal, bread, letters — went on without either of them.

definitions.plain: The warmth of the sun in winter.
definitions.poetic: January’s small mercy: sunlight with its kettle just off the boil.
definitions.riddle: Find me on a freezing day, on the south wall, where the cat already sits.

etymology: From a Latin word for basking in sunshine; recorded once in 1656 and promptly mislaid by the language.
usage: They turned their chairs to the window to borrow a little ___.

definitions.plain: Foggy, misty, and grey, as winter weather.
definitions.poetic: Weather wearing wool: the world gone soft-edged and near-sighted.
definitions.riddle: On my kind of morning the lighthouse earns its keep and the hills go missing.

etymology: From the French for winter mist, tracing back to the Latin name for the year’s shortest day.
usage: The harbour lay ___ and still, the ferries sounding their horns blind.

definitions.plain: Glittering with gold or tinsel; showily sparkling.
definitions.poetic: Dressed in borrowed starlight and pleased about it.
definitions.riddle: I am the glitter of the stage crown — all flash and no jewels.

etymology: From a French verb imitating the chime of coins; English borrowed the shine in the 1590s.
usage: The theatre lobby was ___ with mirrors and gilt.

definitions.plain: A sleepwalker; one who walks about at night.
definitions.poetic: A dreamer whose dreams put on slippers and take the stairs.
definitions.riddle: I climb stairs I never remember and wake up owning cold feet.

etymology: Latin night joined to Latin walking; the doctors preferred the sleep-word for it, and the poets preferred this one.
usage: The old innkeeper, a gentle ___, was found dusting shelves at three in the morning.

definitions.plain: A tiny trace or spark of something.
definitions.poetic: One firefly’s worth of light — and sometimes that is enough to navigate by.
definitions.riddle: Lawyers hunt me in evidence, prospectors in gravel: the least gleam that still counts.

etymology: Latin for a spark; the courtroom borrowed it for the faintest glimmer of proof.
usage: There was not a ___ of doubt in her voice.

definitions.plain: A small fib; pretentious nonsense.
definitions.poetic: A lie in its Sunday best, small enough to curtsy.
definitions.riddle: Not quite a lie, says the teller; quite a lie, says the listener. I am the size of the difference.

etymology: Origin uncertain, perhaps from an old word for dawdling — collected among eighteenth-century slang.
usage: His account of catching the pike grew a fresh ___ with every telling.

definitions.plain: The empty space left in a barrel or bottle that is not quite full.
definitions.poetic: The breath a bottle keeps for itself, between wine and cork.
definitions.riddle: The kinder the pour, the larger I grow — I am what the cask no longer holds.

etymology: From an Old French verb meaning to fill a cask up to the eye — the word came to name what filling leaves behind.
usage: The cellar-master tapped each cask, listening for its ___.

definitions.plain: Of, or happening in, the evening.
definitions.poetic: Belonging to the lamp-lighting hour, when moths take the day shift’s place.
definitions.riddle: Morning glories ignore me; jasmine and owls keep my calendar.

etymology: From the Latin name for the first star of dusk, which also lent its name to the prayers sung at day’s end.
usage: The café kept ___ hours, opening as the streetlights warmed.

definitions.plain: The gap in a hedge made by the regular passage of a small animal.
definitions.poetic: A door in a wall of thorns, cut by nothing but habit.
definitions.riddle: No one made me. Something small simply went the same way often enough.

etymology: A Sussex hedger’s word, collected by dialect societies in the 1870s and then quietly allowed to fall out of the language.
usage: A hare had left a ___ low in the blackthorn.

definitions.plain: Four sheets of paper folded together to make one section of a book.
definitions.poetic: The smallest bundle a book is willing to be built from.
definitions.riddle: Fold me, nest me, sew me to my brothers, and between us we have made a spine.

etymology: From the Latin for ‘four together’, by way of Old French; a printer’s unit for centuries before it was a stationer’s.
usage: He wrote the whole preface in a single ___, then burned two leaves of it.

definitions.plain: Study or writing carried on late into the night, by lamplight.
definitions.poetic: The work that only gets done after the household has gone up, and shows it at breakfast.
definitions.riddle: I smell of hot oil and cold tea, and every preface thanking a patient family is my doing.

etymology: Latin, and reckoned by the lamp: a scholar’s labour was measured in how much oil it had cost.
usage: The dictionary’s third volume was pure ___, and the family scarcely saw him for a year.

definitions.plain: A person employed to write down what another dictates, or to copy their work.
definitions.poetic: The second pair of hands on a great book, named nowhere on its spine.
definitions.riddle: Milton went blind and I finished the poem; Dostoevsky married me. What was my post?

etymology: Latin, from the household slave who served ‘at the hand’ — a Roman job that became a profession and then a courtesy.
usage: He dictated the last entries to an ___ and signed each page with a shaking hand.

definitions.plain: A professional copyist and drafter of documents, before typewriters and solicitors.
definitions.poetic: A whole trade of men paid by the sheet for handwriting worth trusting.
definitions.riddle: I draw up your lease, your will and your love letters in a hand you could not manage, and I charge by the sheet.

etymology: From a Latin verb for writing, by way of Italian and French; the trade had guilds, ledgers and a livery company of its own in London.
usage: The lease was drawn by a ___ whose flourishes take up half the page.

definitions.plain: The note at the end of a book giving the printer, the place, and the date.
definitions.poetic: The printer’s signature, set at the back where only the curious will find it.
definitions.riddle: A title page says what the book is; I say who made it, and I wait until everyone else has left.

etymology: Greek for a finishing stroke — the word for putting the last hand to a thing, taken up by the first printers for their last page.
usage: The ___ records a printer in Ghent and a year that the binding disputes.

definitions.plain: A single term printed at the foot of a page, repeating the first of the next page.
definitions.poetic: A printer’s small insurance against a binder who cannot read.
definitions.riddle: On an old page, the line beneath the last line is not a mistake: it is me, holding the next leaf’s place.

etymology: An English printing term of the seventeenth century; the practice went out with hand-binding, and the name went off to work in politics.
usage: The ___ at the foot of folio twelve does not match the page that follows it.

definitions.plain: The frame on a paper mould that gives a hand-made sheet its rough, soft edge.
definitions.poetic: The reason old paper stops in a feathered fringe instead of a cut line.
definitions.riddle: Machines can only imitate my edge; I am the frame that let the pulp stop where it liked.

etymology: From a German word for a cover or lid, carried into English with the papermaking trade.
usage: The endpapers keep their ___ edge, soft as felt under the thumb.

definitions.plain: The small rust-brown spots that spread across the pages of old books.
definitions.poetic: The freckling that comes to paper with age, and to nothing else in the room.
definitions.riddle: Damp and iron and eighty years give me to a book; a dealer will knock a third off the price for me.

etymology: Booksellers named it for a colour, and the chemistry behind it — damp, mould, or the metal in the paper — is argued over still.
usage: A little ___ on the title page, and otherwise a sound copy.

definitions.plain: The mark that shows where a new paragraph begins — a reversed P with two legs.
definitions.poetic: A gate set in the middle of a line, telling the reader to take a breath and start again.
definitions.riddle: Scribes drew me in red ink and printers stopped drawing me at all; I mean only this: a new thought begins here.

etymology: An English mangling of the Greek-derived term for a paragraph — the word was copied by ear until nobody could see the original inside it.
usage: The rubricator left a space for a ___ on every third line and then never came back.

definitions.plain: The metal band or cap on the end of a stick, tool handle, or pencil.
definitions.poetic: The small brass collar that stops a walking stick from splitting itself on the road.
definitions.riddle: The least considered part of an umbrella, and the first of it to meet the pavement — what am I?

etymology: From a Latin word for a little bracelet, confused early on with the word for iron, which is what most of them are made of.
usage: The stick’s ___ has worn to a wafer on one side from thirty years of the same lane.

definitions.plain: The stiffened tip at the end of a shoelace or cord.
definitions.poetic: A shoelace has exactly one engineered component, and it is the first to give way.
definitions.riddle: Nobody knows my name until I am gone; then the lace frays and the eyelet wins.

etymology: From a French word for a little needle — the point that let a lace be threaded, back when laces held whole outfits together.
usage: The left ___ is gone, and she threads the lace with a licked point instead.

definitions.plain: A clockwork model of the solar system, its planets driven round on brass arms.
definitions.poetic: The heavens reduced to brass, wound with a key and standing on a library table.
definitions.riddle: Turn my handle and a century of nights goes by in a minute, with the moon keeping every appointment.

etymology: Named after the nobleman who commissioned the first one; the instrument-maker’s own name is on none of them.
usage: The ___ has lost Saturn, and the arm that held it swings free.

definitions.plain: The toothed wheel and lever that let a clock’s power out one tick at a time.
definitions.poetic: The part of a clock that refuses to let the weight fall all at once.
definitions.riddle: Tick — one tooth is away. Tock — I have caught the next. Take me out and the clock spends its whole strength in a second.

etymology: A clockmaker’s term from the eighteenth century, when a dozen designs competed and each was named for its own shape: anchor, deadbeat, grasshopper.
usage: The ___ wants oil; you can hear it hesitate before the hour.

definitions.plain: Glowing or flickering softly, without heat; playing lightly over a surface.
definitions.poetic: The blue that runs along the top of a coal fire and touches nothing.
definitions.riddle: I play over a log without burning it, and over a good sentence without raising the voice.

etymology: From a Latin verb for licking — the flame that plays over a surface, and, by the eighteenth century, the wit that plays over a subject.
usage: A ___ light moved on the ceiling where the fire had found the brass.

definitions.plain: Rain that falls from a cloud and dries in the air before it reaches the ground.
definitions.poetic: A grey combing under a cloud, on its way down and never arriving.
definitions.riddle: The desert sees me most: I am a promise a cloud makes and the air takes back.

etymology: Latin for a rod or a slender branch, chosen by meteorologists for the shape the streaks make against the sky.
usage: There was ___ over the hills all afternoon, and not a drop fell on the yard.

definitions.plain: A fruit tree trained flat against a wall in a fixed pattern of arms.
definitions.poetic: A pear tree persuaded, over twenty patient years, to grow in two dimensions.
definitions.riddle: Give me a south wall and a pair of secateurs and I will hand back fruit a fortnight early, in a straight line.

etymology: French, from an Italian word for a shoulder: the tree is set against its support the way a man leans on a rail.
usage: The ___ on the kitchen wall has borne pears since the old man trained it.

definitions.plain: A lane worn so deep by centuries of feet and carts that it runs below the fields.
definitions.poetic: A road that has sunk into the land it crosses, roofed over by the hedges on its banks.
definitions.riddle: Two thousand years of boots and hooves cut me; walk me in June and the light comes down green.

etymology: The name is medieval; the lanes are far older than the name, and some of them were sunk a foot deeper by every century that used them.
usage: The ___ drops below the fields for half a mile and comes up in the churchyard.

definitions.plain: Of the twilight; active at dusk and dawn rather than by day or by night.
definitions.poetic: The hunting hour of moths, bats and owls, when the light is generous to neither eye.
definitions.riddle: Cats keep my hours, and so do deer, and so does every insect a swallow wants.

etymology: From the Latin for failing light, and a naturalist’s word before it was a poet’s — it sorts animals, not moods.
usage: Badgers are ___, which is why the sett looks abandoned all afternoon.

definitions.plain: White ice built up on branches and wires by fog freezing where it touches.
definitions.poetic: Fog turned to feathers on the windward side of every twig, and none at all on the other.
definitions.riddle: My cousin grows on a clear night out of nothing at all; I am built by a fog that froze as it landed.

etymology: Old English, and nearly extinct by the eighteenth century before the poets took it up; weather reports have kept it alive since.
usage: Every wire on the moor carried an inch of ___ on the windward side.

definitions.plain: A dealer in supplies — once in tallow and wax, later in ship’s stores.
definitions.poetic: The tradesman a whole harbour depends on, whose shop smells of tar, rope and hot fat.
definitions.riddle: Two trades wear my name: one lit your evenings, and the other provisioned your voyage.

etymology: A Norman-French trade name that outlived its trade; the surname is far commoner now than the shop.
usage: The ___ on the quay will have oakum, if anyone still does.

definitions.plain: The last of the day’s prayers in a religious house, said before sleep.
definitions.poetic: The office that closes a monastery’s day, sung with the lamps already low.
definitions.riddle: Seven times a day the bell calls; I am the seventh, and after me nobody speaks until morning.

etymology: Named in Latin for the closing of the daily round; the rule that follows it — silence until dawn — is older than the name.
usage: The bell for ___ went at eight, and the house obeyed it out of habit.

definitions.plain: The room in a monastery set aside for copying and illuminating books.
definitions.poetic: A cold room with north light, thirty desks, and no flame permitted anywhere near the parchment.
definitions.riddle: No lamp was allowed in me, so my working day ended exactly when the light did.

etymology: Latin, and monastic; the rule against fire in these rooms is why so many medieval books survive and so few of the copyists stayed warm.
usage: Four hands copied the psalter in the ___, and only one of them could spell.

definitions.plain: Strange and marvellous; rarely seen.
definitions.poetic: So seldom met that the eye must be taught it twice before it will keep.
definitions.riddle: I once described comets and camels to villagers who had seen neither.

etymology: Old English, and one of the words the language dropped when it acquired ‘strange’ from the French.
usage: A ___ light hung above the marsh, and the whole village came out to look.

definitions.plain: The close of the day; the hour when dusk gathers.
definitions.poetic: The day folding its letter and sealing it with a first star.
definitions.riddle: The plough stops, the lamp is lit, and only the older tongue still has a name for me.

etymology: Old English, from a time when the language still measured the day in hours that each had a name of their own.
usage: At ___ the bells rang the fields home.

definitions.plain: The evening that has just gone by; the hours after dark, now past.
definitions.poetic: Last night’s dark, not yet cold in the room it left.
definitions.riddle: Gone a mere handful of hours, and still the ballads mourn me like a whole year.

etymology: A Scots contraction of an older phrase for the night just gone — beloved of Burns and of the border ballads.
usage: ___ the frost came early and silvered all the panes.

definitions.plain: The second day from now: the one that follows the day that follows this.
definitions.poetic: Two sunrises off, and English has stopped keeping a name for it.
definitions.riddle: Let one whole day go by unremarked and I am the next to arrive.

etymology: Middle English, and given up when English stopped keeping single words for the days around today; German still has its twin.
usage: The mended clock will be ready ___, the tinker promised.

definitions.plain: The wishbone of a fowl.
definitions.poetic: The little forked bone that holds a wish until two hands set it free.
definitions.riddle: Two pull; one keeps the longer half and the promise inside it. What bone am I?

etymology: Named for the custom rather than the bird: two diners, one snap, and the winner keeps what was wished.
usage: The cousins dried the ___ on the sill for tomorrow’s tug.

definitions.plain: In a direction against the sun’s course; counterclockwise.
definitions.poetic: The wrong way round the church, where folktales keep their trouble.
definitions.riddle: Walk with me thrice round the well and the stories say you’ll wake the luck you shouldn’t.

etymology: From Middle Low German, ‘against the course’ — the opposite of walking sunwise.
usage: She stirred the pot ___ and her aunt clucked at the omen.

definitions.plain: A cloth laid over the back of a chair to protect it from hair oil.
definitions.poetic: A small linen shield against the greasy heads of the nineteenth century.
definitions.riddle: I exist because gentlemen oiled their hair and their aunts owned good chairs.

etymology: Named for the very hair oil it defended against — a preparation sold as coming from a port in the Indies, and named for that port.
usage: The ___ on the wing-chair has been starched by three generations of housekeepers.

definitions.plain: The roofed entrance to a churchyard, where a bier could be set down out of the rain.
definitions.poetic: A little roof at the edge of the yard, built for waiting in and for nothing else.
definitions.riddle: A shelter with no room, a door with no house — and every village keeps me by the churchyard.

etymology: An Old English word survives in this one structure and nowhere else; Victorian restorers rebuilt half of them in a style that never existed.
usage: They waited under the ___ until the rain had gone through.

definitions.plain: A week, by the reckoning English kept until the eighteenth century.
definitions.poetic: The old unit of a country week: market to market, sermon to sermon.
definitions.riddle: My longer twin still books an English holiday; I have not been spoken since Austen.

etymology: The Germanic peoples counted time in darknesses rather than daylights, which is why an English holiday is still booked by the same arithmetic.
usage: He promised the book in a ___ and delivered it in a year.

definitions.plain: A gift given at the start of a thing — a new year, a new shop, a new coat.
definitions.poetic: The first coin taken in a new shop, kept in the apron and never spent.
definitions.riddle: Pay me to a fishwife on a Monday morning and she will spit on me for luck.

etymology: Old English and Old Norse shared it; in Scotland the first Monday of the year was named for the custom and kept as a holiday within living memory.
usage: She gave the boy a shilling as a ___ on his first day at the forge.

definitions.plain: A painter of miniatures and illuminated letters; an old word for an artist.
definitions.poetic: The man who put the gold leaf on the capital letter and the face into the locket.
definitions.riddle: Before the camera, I was how you knew what your grandmother had looked like.

etymology: A worn form of the word for illumination, from the days when the gold on a manuscript was applied by a specialist.
usage: The ___ was paid in coin and dinner, and left the eyes until last.

definitions.plain: A blunt, thick needle used to draw tape or cord through a hem or a casing.
definitions.poetic: The fat needle at the bottom of the workbox, too blunt to prick and too useful to throw out.
definitions.riddle: Thread me with ribbon and I will find my way through a hem that no finger could.

etymology: Middle English, origin obscure and possibly Celtic; it has meant a dagger, a hairpin and a needle, and settled at last on the needle.
usage: She threaded the elastic with a ___ and a great deal of patience.
